what_its_for: Montelukast is used to help prevent and control asthma symptoms and to relieve symptoms of seasonal allergies (such as runny nose, sneezing, and itchy eyes). It works by blocking certain chemicals in your body that cause swelling and tightening in your airways. It is NOT a rescue inhaler — it will not stop an asthma attack that has already started.
how_to_take: Take montelukast by mouth, with or without food. Swallow tablets whole. If you have chewable tablets, chew them fully before swallowing — do not swallow them whole. Oral granules (powder) can be poured directly into your mouth, mixed with a spoonful of soft food like applesauce, or dissolved in a small amount of baby formula or breast milk. Do not mix granules into liquid other than formula or breast milk. Take it at the same time every day to help you remember. For asthma, take it in the evening. For allergies only, you can take it at any time of day.
dosing: Your doctor will choose the right dose for your age. Typical doses are: Adults and teenagers 15 years and older — one 10 mg tablet once a day. Children 6 to 14 years old — one 5 mg chewable tablet once a day. Children 2 to 5 years old — one 4 mg chewable tablet or one packet of 4 mg granules once a day. Children 12 to 23 months (for asthma only) — one packet of 4 mg granules once a day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next regular dose at the usual time. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store montelukast at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from moisture, heat, and direct sunlight. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Oral granule packets should be used within 15 minutes of opening — do not save an opened packet for later.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking aspirin or anti-inflammatory pain medicines (such as ibuprofen or naproxen) if your doctor has told you that these medicines make your asthma worse. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, since some medicines can affect how montelukast works. Avoid stopping this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel better.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you notice: mood or behavior changes such as agitation, aggression, unusual dreams, trouble sleeping, depression, or thoughts of self-harm or suicide (these are rare but serious side effects); signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing; worsening asthma symptoms or increased need for your rescue inhaler; muscle pain or weakness; tremors or shaking. This medicine has a serious FDA warning (called a Boxed Warning) about mental health side effects — talk to your doctor if you have any concerns.
when_it_works: Montelukast may start to improve your symptoms within a day or two, but it may take up to a few weeks to feel the full benefit. Keep taking it every day as directed, even when you feel well. It works best when taken consistently over time.
special_populations: Children: Montelukast is approved for children as young as 12 months for asthma and 2 years for allergies. Use the correct dose and form (granules or chewable tablets) based on your child's age and weight as directed by your doctor. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before taking montelukast if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks for you and your baby. Older adults: No special dose adjustment is typically needed for older adults, but always follow your doctor's guidance. Liver disease: Tell your doctor if you have liver problems, as your dose may need to be adjusted.
